title: Week 9: Visualization, Decision Support and Data Quality
overview: Learn how health data become trustworthy and useful for decision-making. Examine accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness; explore structured and unstructured records, NLP, metadata, missing data, cleaning and visualization; and connect dashboards and the five rights of decision support to healthcare workflows.
objectives: Explain data-quality dimensions and their effects on reliable decisions.
Compare structured and unstructured health data, including NLP limitations.
Describe metadata, data cleaning, missing-value decisions and exploratory checks.
Select bar charts, line charts, histograms, tables and text summaries appropriately.
Explain dashboard use and the five rights of clinical decision support.

concepts.name: Data quality
concepts.definition: The degree to which data are fit for their intended purpose.

concepts.name: Accuracy
concepts.definition: A recorded value correctly represents the patient, event, measurement or condition.

concepts.name: Completeness
concepts.definition: Required information is present for the intended use.

concepts.name: Consistency
concepts.definition: Comparable data use compatible definitions, categories, formats and units.

concepts.name: Timeliness
concepts.definition: Data are current and available when needed.

concepts.name: Structured data
concepts.definition: Data in defined fields and controlled formats, suitable for querying, counts and comparisons.

concepts.name: Unstructured data
concepts.definition: Narrative notes, images, audio and free text without a simple fixed field structure.

concepts.name: Natural language processing
concepts.definition: Methods that make human-language data usable by computers, while requiring care with negation, timing and uncertainty.

concepts.name: Metadata
concepts.definition: Information about information, such as definitions, units, sources, dates, codes and versions.

concepts.name: Data cleaning
concepts.definition: Checking for impossible, duplicated, inconsistent or incorrectly coded values.

concepts.name: Missing data
concepts.definition: Data that are not asked, known, applicable or entered.

concepts.name: Imputation
concepts.definition: Replacing a missing value using a defined and documented method.

concepts.name: Descriptive quality checks
concepts.definition: Counts, percentages, averages, ranges, distributions and crosstabs used to investigate data quality.

concepts.name: Data visualization
concepts.definition: A purposeful display of patterns, comparisons, trends and distributions.

concepts.name: Bar chart
concepts.definition: A chart used to compare categories or groups.

concepts.name: Line chart
concepts.definition: A chart used to show changes across time.

concepts.name: Histogram
concepts.definition: A chart used to show the distribution of a numerical variable.

concepts.name: Table
concepts.definition: An organized display of exact values, with clear headings, units, timeframe and source.

concepts.name: Exploratory data analysis
concepts.definition: Understanding the shape, patterns, relationships and plausible limits of data before formal analysis.

concepts.name: Dashboard
concepts.definition: A collection of selected measures to support monitoring and action.

concepts.name: Clinical decision support
concepts.definition: Patient-specific or situation-specific information that supports a healthcare decision.

concepts.name: Five rights of clinical decision support
concepts.definition: The right information, person, format, channel and time.

concepts.name: Big data
concepts.definition: Data often described by high volume, velocity and variety.

sections.title: 1. Why quality affects trust
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores data quality determines whether results can be trusted and ask quality questions before using data. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Data quality determines whether results can be trusted (original slide 2).
• Data quality describes how well data are fit for their intended use.
• Poor data can create incorrect counts, misleading trends, and inappropriate recommendations.
• Quality should be considered when data are collected, entered, stored, exchanged, analyzed, and presented.
• A data-quality problem may require correction, clarification, exclusion, or a clear limitation statement.
• Good analysis cannot fully compensate for data that do not represent the situation accurately.

Ask quality questions before using data (original slide 3).
• For what purpose were the data originally collected?
• How were the data collected, entered, coded, and changed over time?
• Are definitions, units, categories, and standards clear?
• Which fields are missing, duplicated, delayed, or implausible?
• How will the data be analyzed and presented so that users can interpret them correctly?

sections.title: 2. Quality questions before use
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores accuracy and completeness are basic quality dimensions and consistency and timeliness matter too. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Accuracy and completeness are basic quality dimensions (original slide 4).
• Accuracy means that a value correctly represents the patient, event, measurement, or condition.
• Completeness means that required information is present for the intended use.
• An accurate but incomplete record may still lead to an unsafe or biased conclusion.
• Examples of missing information include absent allergies, incomplete outcomes, or an unrecorded result.
• Quality checks should focus on fields that affect care, reporting, or decisions.

Consistency and timeliness matter too (original slide 5).
• Consistency means that the same concept, unit, category, or rule is used in comparable records.
• Timeliness means that information is available and current when it is needed.
• A delayed result may be accurate but not useful for a time-sensitive decision.
• Inconsistent categories can make two departments appear different when they recorded the same event differently.
• Quality dimensions should be judged against the purpose and timeframe of the use.

sections.title: 3. Data quality dimensions
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores collection choices shape data quality and structured data are easy to compute. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Collection choices shape data quality (original slide 6).
• Organizations should decide why data are being entered and which fields are necessary.
• The data-entry method should fit the user, setting, workflow, and type of information.
• Required fields and controlled values can improve consistency but may reduce flexibility.
• Free text can preserve detail but may be harder to search, count, or compare.
• Training and feedback help users understand how their documentation affects later use.

Structured data are easy to compute (original slide 7).
• Structured data use defined fields, formats, and controlled values.
• Examples include a coded diagnosis, a date field, a numeric measurement, or a selected category.
• Structured data are easier to query, count, compare, and use in analytics.
• Rigid choices can omit nuance or force users to select an imperfect category.
• Good design balances computability with the clinical meaning users need to record.

sections.title: 4. Collection choices and structured data
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores unstructured data preserve narrative detail and nlp can make narrative data more usable. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Unstructured data preserve narrative detail (original slide 8).
• Unstructured data include narrative notes, free text, images, audio, and other content without a fixed field structure.
• Narrative documentation can express context, uncertainty, timing, and patient experience.
• It is more difficult to search and analyze directly than structured data.
• Natural language processing can help identify concepts, but negation and temporal meaning remain challenging.
• Many healthcare environments need both structured fields and meaningful narrative.

NLP can make narrative data more usable (original slide 9).
• Natural language processing, or NLP, converts human language into information that computer systems can manipulate.
• NLP may help identify diagnoses, symptoms, medications, findings, or public-health signals in narrative text.
• It can support patient care, biosurveillance, research, and administrative work.
• A system must distinguish whether a concept is present, absent, historical, planned, or uncertain.
• NLP outputs should be validated before they are used for important decisions.

sections.title: 5. Unstructured information and NLP
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores metadata explains what data mean and cleaning identifies errors and unusual values. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Metadata explains what data mean (original slide 10).
• Metadata are descriptive details about other data.
• Examples include a field definition, unit, source system, collection date, coding system, or version.
• Metadata help users understand how data were created and whether they are suitable for a purpose.
• They support reliability, quality review, reproducibility, and investigation.
• Without metadata, two fields with similar names may be incorrectly treated as equivalent.

Cleaning identifies errors and unusual values (original slide 11).
• Data cleaning checks for impossible, inconsistent, duplicated, or incorrectly coded values.
• Descriptive statistics can reveal unusual ranges, extreme values, and unexpected distributions.
• Crosstabs can show patterns that suggest a data-entry or coding problem.
• The correct value should be verified from a reliable source when possible.
• If an error cannot be corrected, the decision to exclude or retain the record should be documented.

sections.title: 6. Metadata and cleaning
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores missing data require a documented decision and descriptive checks help find quality problems. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Missing data require a documented decision (original slide 12).
• Missingness may occur because a field was not asked, not known, not applicable, or not entered.
• Removing records can reduce the sample and may introduce bias.
• A coded value for missing data should not be mistaken for a real measurement.
• Imputation replaces a missing value using a defined rule, such as a median or another model-based estimate.
• The chosen approach and its possible effect on results should be reported.

Descriptive checks help find quality problems (original slide 13).
• Counts and percentages can reveal unexpected categories or large amounts of missing data.
• Means, medians, ranges, and distributions can reveal implausible continuous values.
• Crosstabs compare categories and can identify inconsistent combinations.
• A review of merged data should check new fields, derived values, timeframes, and changing definitions.
• Analysts should ask whether counts, sums, and averages make sense in the clinical setting.

sections.title: 7. Missingness and descriptive checks
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores visualization helps users see patterns and choose a chart that fits the question. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Visualization helps users see patterns (original slide 14).
• A visualization can show the shape of data, trends, skew, outliers, and missing information.
• Charts can make comparisons easier than a long list of numbers.
• A visualization should answer a defined question rather than decorate the data.
• Labels, units, timeframes, denominators, and sources help users interpret the display.
• The same data can support different conclusions when the scale or grouping is changed.

Choose a chart that fits the question (original slide 15).
• Use a bar chart to compare categories or groups.
• Use a line chart to show change over time.
• Use a histogram to show the distribution of a numeric variable.
• Use a table when exact values or several related fields must be read together.
• Use a text summary when one clear sentence communicates the result better than a graphic.

sections.title: 8. Exploratory visualization
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores clear visuals avoid distortion and tables should stand on their own. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Clear visuals avoid distortion (original slide 16).
• The visual size of a number or percentage should be proportional to the quantity represented.
• Axes should be labeled clearly and scaled honestly.
• Abbreviations should be explained when they may confuse the audience.
• Color should support meaning and remain understandable when printed or viewed by people with color- vision differences.
• Text, capitalization, and font size should make the chart easy to read.

Tables should stand on their own (original slide 17).
• A table should be a logical unit that a reader can understand without searching elsewhere.
• The title, row headings, column headings, units, and timeframe should be understandable.
• The source of the data should be identified.
• Blank cells should be distinguished from zero, not applicable, or missing values.
• Consistent formatting helps readers compare cells without confusion.

sections.title: 9. Choosing appropriate visual displays
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores exploratory analysis checks whether the story makes sense and dashboards connect information to action. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Exploratory analysis checks whether the story makes sense (original slide 18).
• Exploratory data analysis combines descriptive statistics, relationships, and visualization.
• It helps analysts understand the data before applying more formal methods.
• After merging data, review new variables, derived values, timeframes, and values that may change over time.
• Check whether the analysis is correct and whether the outputs are plausible.
• Exploration can reveal questions that require better data or a revised analysis plan.

Dashboards connect information to action (original slide 19).
• A dashboard brings selected measures together so users can monitor a situation.
• A useful dashboard shows the right information to the right people in a form they can understand.
• Users need definitions, timeframes, comparison points, and alerts that support a real workflow.
• Too many measures, unclear scales, or low-quality data can distract or mislead.
• A dashboard should lead to a question, review, or action—not replace thinking.

sections.title: 10. Clear charts and standalone tables
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores decision support uses information at the right moment and big data increases both opportunity and responsibility. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Decision support uses information at the right moment (original slide 20).
• Clinical decision support provides patient-specific or situation-specific information to support a healthcare decision.
• Examples include medication warnings, preventive-care reminders, order guidance, and prompts for missing information.
• The five rights are the right information, person, format, channel, and time.
• Decision support works better when data are accurate, relevant, and integrated into workflow.
• Users must interpret the information and decide what action is appropriate.

Big data increases both opportunity and responsibility (original slide 21).
• Big data is often described by high volume, high velocity, and high variety.
• Healthcare data may combine records, claims, devices, registries, images, and other sources.
• More data do not automatically mean better evidence.
• Different sources may use different definitions, populations, timeframes, and quality controls.
• Large-scale analysis requires careful governance, documentation, privacy protection, and validation.

sections.title: 11. Dashboards and decision support
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores key terms to know and study questions. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Key terms to know (original slide 22).
• Data quality: how well data fit their intended use.
• Accuracy: whether a value correctly represents what it describes.
• Completeness: whether required information is present.
• Consistency: whether comparable data use compatible definitions and formats.
• Timeliness: whether information is available and current when needed.
• Visualization: a purposeful display that helps users interpret data.

Study questions (original slide 23).
• What is the difference between data and information?
• Distinguish descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics.
• What are the main steps in a healthcare analytics workflow?
• Why do accuracy, completeness, consistency, and timeliness matter?
• Compare structured and unstructured data, including one strength and one limitation of each.
• How can a visualization or dashboard help a healthcare user make a decision?
• What are the five rights of clinical decision support?

sections.title: 12. Big data and integrated review
sections.body:
This part of the lecture explores final summary. Read each point alongside its original source page and consider how it affects healthcare decisions and workflows.

Final summary (original slide 24).
• Healthcare analytics turns data into information that can support care, operations, quality, and planning.
• The four analytics types answer different questions: what happened, why, what may happen, and what action may help.
• Data quality and metadata determine whether an analysis is meaningful and trustworthy.
• Clear visualizations and dashboards help users see patterns and connect information to decisions.
• Decision support is most useful when it is accurate, timely, understandable, and reviewed by responsible professionals.

quiz.question: What is data quality?
options: The number of columns in a spreadsheet.
Whether data are fit for their intended use.
quiz.rationale: Quality describes suitability and trustworthiness for a purpose.

quiz.question: What does accuracy measure?
options: Whether a recorded value represents the event correctly.
Whether two systems use the same format.

quiz.question: What does completeness measure?
options: Whether two codes use identical definitions.
quiz.rationale: Completeness concerns presence of required data.

quiz.question: What does consistency address?
options: Whether an individual reading is correct.
Compatible definitions, categories and units across comparable records.
How many users view a report.

quiz.question: What does metadata describe?
options: A guarantee that all values are accurate.
Definitions, units, source, date, coding system and version.
quiz.rationale: Metadata help explain how to interpret and use recorded data.

quiz.question: How should missing data be handled?
options: Investigate and document their cause and handling approach.
Assume missing values are negative findings.
quiz.rationale: Deleting or imputing records can affect results and should be documented.

quiz.question: Which chart is best for showing change over time?
options: A table of only patient IDs
A pie chart without category labels
quiz.rationale: Line charts show trends through time.

quiz.question: Which display shows the distribution of a numeric variable?
quiz.rationale: A histogram shows the frequency distribution of numeric measurements.

quiz.question: Which is one of the five rights of clinical decision support?
options: Show every alert to every user.
Deliver the right information to the right person at the right time.
Delay an alert until after the decision.
quiz.rationale: The rights cover information, person, format, channel and time.

quiz.question: What makes a dashboard useful?
options: Relevant, well-defined measures shown in support of a real workflow.
Using arbitrary axes to emphasize small changes.
quiz.rationale: A useful dashboard connects comprehensible, reliable measures to appropriate action.
